description: We are Selene Nav, we possess skills in web development and programming, along with dedication, creativity, and versatility in solving the challenges presented to us.
summary:
Lunaris is an interactive decision-support tool built for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge at the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Near the lunar south pole, the Sun skims the horizon and rugged terrain casts long shadows that block both solar power generation and direct-to-Earth communication. Lunaris addresses this operational challenge by combining a Python data pipeline with a self-contained, web application to compare candidate landing sites and mission dates.   
Our pipeline ingests real ephemeris data from the NASA/JPL Horizons API (accounting for lunar libration) and laser altimetry terrain models from LRO/LOLA to compute 360° local horizon profiles and run automated physics validation checks. Through an intuitive interface featuring both educational (Explore) and engineering (Plan) modes, users can interact with a 3D Moon globe, compare up to four mission scenarios side by side (including the nine official Artemis III candidate regions), simulate launch delays, inspect 360° sky panoramas with real terrain toggles, and find optimal landing windows via interactive heatmaps.
details:
**What does it do and how does it work?**

Selene Nav is a web app that answers, in seconds, the two questions that decide whether a lunar landing survives: *will the lander have sunlight for power, and will Earth be in view for direct communication?* It focuses on the Moon's south pole, where the Sun never rises more than about 1.5° above the horizon and a single distant mountain can cut a lander's power.

Users start on an interactive 3D Moon with Apollo sites, commercial CLPS landers, missions from other countries and the 9 Artemis candidate regions. They pick a site and a landing date, and compare up to four plans side by side. Each plan gets a clear verdict (good, caution or not recommended) with the reason, the share of time with sunlight and with Earth in view, and countdowns to sunset and Earthset. A "What if the launch slips?" control delays the landing by one week, two weeks or a month and shows the before and after instantly.

Other views explain the result:

- a 360° panorama of the real horizon with the Sun and Earth paths;

- a shaded south pole map ranking nearby sites for the same date;

- a Sun-elevation chart against the terrain;

- a calendar that highlights the best landing days.

Behind it, a Python pipeline downloads Sun and Earth positions for every site from NASA/JPL Horizons. It builds a 360° horizon for each site from LRO LOLA terrain, including the Moon's curvature, and treats the Sun as a disk to compute how much of it clears the mountains. Five physics checks validate the data, and all of them pass. For example, the Sun never exceeds ~1.5° at the pole, and Earth is never visible from the Chang'e 4 far-side site.

**What are the benefits?**

The data needed to plan a landing already exists, but tools such as Horizons, Quickmap and Moon Trek are built for specialists and require jumping between interfaces and reading raw numbers. Selene Nav turns that data into answers anyone can compare:

- **Mission planners** can re-evaluate sites and dates quickly when hardware delays or launch slips change the schedule.

- **Educators, students and the public** can see why the lunar south pole is so hard to land on.

The app runs in any browser with no install or login, works on mobile, and is available in English and Portuguese.

**What is the intended impact?**

Faster, clearer decisions in the early stages of lunar mission planning, and better communication between science and engineering teams. It also opens a window for students to understand real exploration constraints. The same approach can extend to other sites, other bodies such as Mars, and additional constraints such as eclipses and ground-station schedules.

**Tools, languages, hardware and software**

- **Python** (numpy) for the data pipeline: ephemeris download, horizon computation from LOLA terrain, map rendering and validation.

- **HTML, CSS and JavaScript** for the web app, in a single file with no external libraries. The 3D Moon and every chart are drawn by our own code.

- **NASA data and tools:** JPL Horizons API, LRO LOLA polar DEMs, LROC Quickmap, NASA Moon Trek. **Partner agency:** CSA Moon Exploration.

- **GitHub and GitHub Pages** for source code and hosting.

- **An AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic)** helped with research, code, design and text. All scientific numbers come from NASA data.

- Standard laptops; no special hardware.

**How is the project creative?**

Instead of another viewer for raw data, Selene Nav makes the result the interface: a colored verdict, a reason in plain words and a countdown. Features that existing tools do not offer:

- the launch-slip simulation;

- a toggle that removes the mountains to show how much terrain matters;

- a best-date calendar;

- a map that ranks alternative sites for the same date.

It also explains the physics in plain language with a guided tour and a glossary. Explore mode is for the public; Plan mode, with editable mission rules and CSV export, is for engineers.

**What factors did the team consider?**

- **Scientific accuracy:** real terrain instead of a flat horizon, no atmospheric refraction, the Sun as a disk, libration included, and validation tests shown in the app.

- **Honesty about limits:** Earth in view does not guarantee contact, terrain uncertainty affects exact times near the pole, the Artemis coordinates are approximate, eclipses are not modeled, and the 3D Moon is illustrative. All of this is stated in the app.

- **Usability:** plain language, a guided tour, mobile support and no setup for the user.

- **Global audience:** English by default, Portuguese available.

- **Real-world planning needs:** schedule slips, comparing alternatives and clear criteria that planners can adjust.
